exercise_group.instructions: Mark each statement True or False. Justify each answer. In each part, $A$ represents an $n \times n$ matrix.

statement.paragraph: (T/F) If $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable, then $A$ is symmetric.
(T/F) If $A$ is an orthogonal matrix, then $A$ is symmetric.
(T/F) If $A$ is an orthogonal matrix, then $\text{∥}\textit{A}\textbf{x}\text{∥} = \text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥}$ for all $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.
(T/F) The principal axes of a quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ can be the columns of any matrix $P$ that diagonalizes $A$.
(T/F) If $P$ is an $n \times n$ matrix with orthogonal columns, then $P^{T} = P^{- 1}$.
(T/F) If every coefficient in a quadratic form is positive, then the quadratic form is positive definite.
(T/F) If $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x} > 0$ for some $\textbf{x}$, then the quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is positive definite.
(T/F) By a suitable change of variable, any quadratic form can be changed into one with no cross-product term.
(T/F) The largest value of a quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$, for $\text{∥}\textbf{x}\text{∥} = 1$, is the largest entry on the diagonal of $A$.
(T/F) The maximum value of a positive definite quadratic form $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ is the greatest eigenvalue of $A$.
(T/F) A positive definite quadratic form can be changed into a negative definite form by a suitable change of variable $\textbf{x} = P\textbf{u}$, for some orthogonal matrix $P$.
(T/F) An indefinite quadratic form is one whose eigenvalues are not definite.
(T/F) If $P$ is an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix, then the change of variable $\textbf{x} = P\textbf{u}$ transforms $\textbf{x}^{T}A\textbf{x}$ into a quadratic form whose matrix is $P^{- 1}{AP}$.
(T/F) If $U$ is $m \times n$ with orthogonal columns, then $UU^{T}\textbf{x}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{x}$ onto $\text{Col\,\,\,}U$.
(T/F) If $B$ is $m \times n$ and $\textbf{x}$ is a unit vector in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, then $\text{∥}\textit{B}\textbf{x}\text{∥} \leq \sigma_{1}$, where $\sigma_{1}$ is the first singular value of $B$.

(T/F) A singular value decomposition of an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ can be written as $B = P\text{Σ}Q$, where $P$ is an $m \times m$ orthogonal matrix, $Q$ is an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix, and $\text{Σ}$ is an $m \times n$ “diagonal” matrix.
(T/F) If $A$ is $n \times n$, then $A$ and $A^{T}A$ have the same singular values.
Let $\{\textbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{u}_{n}\}$ be an orthonormal basis for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, and let $\text{λ}_{1},\ldots,\text{λ}_{n}$ be any real scalars. Define

list.item: Show that λ1,…,λn are the eigenvalues of A.

statement.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix of rank $r$. Explain why the spectral decomposition of $A$ represents $A$ as the sum of $r~\text{rank\,\,}1$ matrices.
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix.

list.item: Show that (Col A)⊥=Nul A. [Hint: See Section 6.1.]
Show that each y in ℝn can be written in the form y=yˆ+z, with yˆ in Col A and z in Nul A.

statement.paragraph: Show that if $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ and $\mathbf{v}$ corresponds to a nonzero eigenvalue of $A$, then $\mathbf{v}$ is in $\text{Col\,\,}A$. [Hint:Use the definition of an eigenvector.]
Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ symmetric matrix. Use Exercise 21 and an eigenvector basis for $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ to give a second proof of the decomposition in Exercise 20(b).

Prove that an $n \times n$ matrix $A$ is positive definite if and only if $A$ admits a Cholesky factorization, namely $A = R^{T}R$ for some invertible upper triangular matrix $R$ whose diagonal entries are all positive. [Hint:Use a $QR$ factorization and Exercise 34 in Section 7.2.]
Use Exercise 23 to show that if $A$ is positive definite, then $A$ has an $LU$ factorization, $A = LU$, where $U$ has positive pivots on its diagonal. (The converse is true, too.)

exercise_group.instructions: If $A$ is $m \times n$, then the matrix $G = A^{T}A$ is called the Gram matrix of$A$. In this case, the entries of $G$ are the inner products of the columns of $A$. (See Exercises 25 and 26.)

statement.paragraph: Show that the Gram matrix of any matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite, with the same rank as $A$. (See the Exercises in Section 6.5.)

Show that if an $n \times n$ matrix $G$ is positive semidefinite and has $\text{rank~}r$, then $G$ is the Gram matrix of some $r \times n$ matrix $A$. This is called a rank-revealing factorization of $G$. [Hint:Consider the spectral decomposition of $G$, and first write $G$ as $BB^{T}$ for an $n \times r$ matrix $B$.]

Prove that any $n \times n$ matrix $A$ admits a polar decomposition of the form $A = PQ$, where $P$ is an $n \times n$ positive semidefinite matrix with the same rank as $A$ and where $Q$ is an $n \times n$ orthogonal matrix. [Hint:Use a singular value decomposition, $A = U\text{Σ}V^{T}$, and observe that $A = (U\text{Σ}U^{T})(UV^{T})$.] This decomposition is used, for instance, in mechanical engineering to model the deformation of a material. The matrix $P$ describes the stretching or compression of the material (in the directions of the eigenvectors of $P$), and $Q$ describes the rotation of the material in space.

exercise_group.instructions: Exercises 28–30 concern an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ with a reduced singular value decomposition, $A = U_{r}DV_{r}^{T}$, and the pseudoinverse $A^{+} = V_{r}D^{- 1}U_{r}^{T}$.

statement.paragraph: Verify the properties of $A^{+}$:

list.item: For each y in ℝm, AA+y is the orthogonal projection of y onto Col A.
For each x in ℝn, A+Ax is the orthogonal projection of x onto Row A.

statement.paragraph: Suppose the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is consistent, and let $\textbf{x}^{+} = A^{+}\textbf{b}$. By Exercise 31 in Section 6.3, there is exactly one vector $\textbf{p}$ in $\text{Row\,\,}A$ such that $A\textbf{p} = \textbf{b}$. The following steps prove that $\textbf{x}^{+} = \textbf{p}$ and $\textbf{x}^{+}$ is the minimum length solution of $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$.

list.item: Show that x+ is in Row A. [Hint: Write b as Ax for some x, and use Exercise 28.]
Show that x+ is a solution of Ax=b.
Show that if u is any solution of Ax=b, then ∥x+∥≤∥u∥, with equality only if u=x+.

statement.paragraph: Given any $\textbf{b}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{m}$, adapt Exercise 28 to show that $A^{+}\textbf{b}$ is the least-squares solution of minimum length. [Hint:Consider the equation $A\textbf{x} = \widehat{\textbf{b}}$, where $\widehat{\textbf{b}}$ is the orthogonal projection of $\textbf{b}$ onto $\text{Col\,\,\,}A.$]

exercise_group.instructions: [T] In Exercises 31 and 32, construct the pseudoinverse of $A$. Begin by using a matrix program to produce the SVD of $A$, or, if that is not available, begin with an orthogonal diagonalization of $A^{T}A$. Use the pseudoinverse to solve $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$, for $\textbf{b} = (6, - 1, - 4,6)$, and let $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ be the solution. Make a calculation to verify that $\widehat{\textbf{x}}$ is in $\text{Row}A$. Find a nonzero vector $\textbf{u}$ in $\text{Nul\,\,}A$, and verify that $\text{∥}\widehat{\textbf{x}}\text{∥} < \text{∥}\widehat{\textbf{x}} + \textbf{u}\text{∥}$, which must be true by Exercise 29(c).
